assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Sterilising
items.clue: Treating water so that microbes in it are killed, making the water safe to drink.

items.label: Sewage sludge
items.clue: The settled solid produced by sedimentation, which is treated by anaerobic digestion.

items.label: Effluent
items.clue: The liquid produced by sedimentation, which is treated by aerobic biological treatment.

items.label: Desalination
items.clue: Removing dissolved salts from salty water or sea water so that it can be used as potable water.

questions.stem: Why is potable water not described as pure water in the chemical sense?

options.text: Because it still contains some dissolved substances
Because it has not been boiled before it is drunk
Because pure water simply means water that is clean and safe
Because a small number of microbes are always left in it

questions.explanation: Potable water contains dissolved substances, so it is a mixture and not chemically pure.

questions.stem: Why may industrial waste water need treatment that sewage does not?

options.text: Because it is always released straight into the rivers
Because it contains no organic matter at all
Because only industrial waste contains harmful microbes
Because it may contain harmful chemicals as well

questions.explanation: The specification says industrial waste water may require removal of organic matter and harmful chemicals.

questions.stem: What does the specification say drinking water should have for humans?

options.text: No dissolved salts and no microbes whatsoever in it
Low levels of dissolved salts and microbes
Only water molecules, with everything else removed
Dissolved salts removed but microbes are left in

questions.explanation: The specification states drinking water should have sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of screening and grit removal at a sewage works?

options.text: To remove large solid objects and the grit
To kill the harmful microbes present in the sewage
To take the dissolved substances out of sewage
To digest the organic matter without any oxygen

questions.explanation: Screening and grit removal takes out large solid objects and grit at the start of treatment.

questions.stem: Why do the methods used to produce potable water differ from one country to another?

options.text: Because the same standard process is used in every country
Because sea water is the cheapest source in every country
Because some sources already look clean enough to drink
Because they depend on available supplies and local conditions

questions.explanation: The specification states that the methods depend on available supplies of water and local conditions.

questions.stem: What two things does sedimentation produce during sewage treatment?

options.text: Solid effluent at the base and liquid sludge above
Microbes at the base and dissolved solids above
Sewage sludge, which settles, and effluent above it
Leachate solution and ash containing compounds

questions.explanation: Sedimentation produces sewage sludge as the settled solid and effluent as the liquid.

questions.stem: In the UK, what is the first step in producing most potable water?

options.text: Choosing an appropriate source of fresh water
Desalinating sea water taken from around the coast
Adding chlorine into the water at the source
Distilling sea water because supplies are unlimited

questions.explanation: The specification lists choosing an appropriate source of fresh water as the first step.

questions.stem: Which statement about the biological stages of sewage treatment is correct?

options.text: Sludge is treated aerobically and effluent anaerobically
The effluent from sedimentation is digested anaerobically
The microbes are removed when the sludge is screened
Sludge is digested anaerobically and effluent treated aerobically

questions.explanation: The specification lists anaerobic digestion of sewage sludge and aerobic biological treatment of effluent.

questions.stem: Why is water passed through filter beds during treatment?

options.text: To kill the microbes in the water before it is drunk
To remove the insoluble solids and large particles
To take the dissolved salts out of the water supply
To lower the pH of the water before it is stored

questions.explanation: Filter beds physically remove insoluble solids and larger particles.

questions.stem: Rank waste water, ground water and salt water by how easily potable water is obtained from them, easiest first.

options.text: Ground water, then waste water, then salt water
Salt water first, then ground water, then waste water
Waste water, then salt water, and ground water last
All three of them are equally easy to treat

questions.explanation: Ground water needs only filtering and sterilising; waste water needs more stages; salt water needs desalination.

questions.stem: What is achieved by the sterilising step in water treatment?

options.text: The grit and larger insoluble particles are taken out
The dissolved salts in the water are removed from it
Harmful microbes present in the water are killed
The water becomes chemically pure and contains only H2O

questions.explanation: Sterilising kills microbes so that the water is safe to drink.

questions.stem: Which set of sterilising agents for potable water is given in the specification?

options.text: Chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light are all used
Chlorine and ozone only, as light adds nothing
Sand, gravel and fine activated charcoal beds
Sodium chloride and dilute sulfuric acid

questions.explanation: These are the three sterilising agents the specification names.

questions.stem: Why are new methods of extracting copper from low-grade ores being developed?

options.text: Because recycling means ore supplies can never run out
Because the copper ores left are becoming scarce
Because low-grade ores give the highest yields of metal
Because traditional mining cannot extract any copper

questions.explanation: The Earth's resources of metal ores are limited and copper ores are becoming scarce.

options.text: Bacteria break down the rock and leave copper metal behind
Plants absorb copper metal and store it in their leaves
Rock is dug up, moved and then disposed of in large heaps
The plants absorb metal compounds and are then burned to give ash

questions.explanation: The specification states that plants absorb metal compounds, are harvested and burned to give ash containing metal compounds.

questions.stem: What do the bacteria used in bioleaching produce?

options.text: Leachate solutions containing metal compounds
Pure copper metal that is left behind in the rock
Copper metal stored inside the plant leaves
A copper oxide gas released into the air

questions.explanation: Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds.

questions.stem: Scrap iron is added to a solution of a copper compound. What happens and why?

options.text: The copper displaces the iron because copper is more reactive
Iron displaces the copper because iron is more reactive
Nothing happens because the two metals are equally reactive
The iron is electrolysed at the positive electrode

questions.explanation: Iron is above copper in the reactivity series, so iron displaces copper from the solution.

questions.stem: A student compares phytomining with traditional mining of copper. Which comparison is valid?

options.text: Phytomining yields pure copper metal without further processing
Phytomining works best on the richest high-grade copper ores
Phytomining avoids moving large amounts of the rock
Phytomining removes the need to use any energy at all

questions.explanation: The specification says these methods avoid digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock.
